title: Mixed-integer optimization with constraint learning
contribution: Embeds trained ML models (linear models, linear SVMs, trees, forests, boosting, ReLU MLPs) learned from decision-outcome data as MIO constraints and objectives, guarded by a convex-hull trust region (clustering, column selection, epsilon enlargement) and an ensemble violation limit; released as OptiCL and tested on WFP food baskets and chemotherapy regimens.
problem_entry: DA+IO (ML and RO as devices; AP testbeds): MIO needs explicit functions, but outcomes such as chemotherapy toxicity or diet palatability cannot be written as functions of the decision although data relate them (p. 2); earlier work fixed one learner per function (p. 4), JANOS/EML are restricted (p. 4), and prescriptive analytics plugs in predictions instead of embedding models (p. 5); model M(w) with y = h_D(x, w) and trust region X(w) (eq. (1), pp. 6-7).
key_idea: Write the trained model itself into the MIO and optimize over it (pp. 5, 9), choosing the learner class per outcome by cross-validation (pp. 5, 31), and guard against learning error with a data convex-hull trust region (pp. 13-15, 18) and an alpha-of-P ensemble violation limit (p. 17), because a misspecified learned constraint can make solutions infeasible (pp. 5-6, 34).
assumptions: Known f and g, discussion mainly linear (p. 7); MIO-representable learners with linear constraints, linear SVMs only (pp. 9, 42); continuous x-hat for the hull (p. 14); no unobserved confounding (p. 29); independent toxicity groups and multiple imputation (pp. 57-58); WFP palatability simulated from experts' suggestions, 121,589 samples of 25 features (pp. 19, 22, 53); 495 trial arms reduced to 320 train / 96 test with a 2008 temporal split, hull over x only (pp. 30-31, 57-58).
proof_devices: Tree embedding: one binary per leaf with big-M split constraints (eqs. (8a)-(8c), p. 43); each split's M computed by maximizing the split expression over known constraints and the trust region (eq. (9), p. 44)
Decomposition by feasible leaf when a tree is the only learned constraint: parallel subproblems, LOs when x is continuous (pp. 11-12; App. A.2 pp. 44-45, one LO 1.8 s)
ReLU big-M built layer by layer (eqs. (10a)-(10e), p. 45); sigmoid output replaced by the logit threshold ln(tau/(1-tau)) and softmax by an argmax big-M (eqs. (11a)-(11b), p. 46)

Convex-hull trust region by convex-combination weights, avoiding facet enumeration (eq. (2), p. 14); union of cluster hulls with one binary per cluster (eq. (3), p. 14); epsilon-CH with p in {1, 2, inf} to keep the class (eq. (5), p. 18)
Ensemble violation limit (1/P) sum I(y_i <= tau) >= 1 - alpha with big-M indicators (eq. (4), p. 17); big-M-free special cases alpha = 0 and the mean constraint (p. 47)

Column selection: restricted master over a subset of points, reduced costs from the KKT stationarity of the Wolfe dual (eqs. (12)-(15), pp. 49-50); Wolfe rather than Fenchel duality, Dantzig-Wolfe without a dual solve in the linear case (pp. 48-49)

Lemma 1: the point with the most negative reduced cost is a vertex of CH(Z), since pricing is an LP over the hull (pp. 50-51); stated for convex, continuously differentiable problems, not combined with branch and bound (pp. 15, 24)
Function learning vs indicator-function learning of a bounded outcome (p. 9)
experiments: WFP (Gurobi v9.1, i7-8665U, 16 GB; pp. 22-23): validation MSE vs MSE at 100 optimal solutions without/with trust region (e.g. CART 0.014 / 0.273 / 0.059; MLP 0.001 / 0.055 / 0.001) and times (LR 0.003 s -> 1.813 s) (Table 5, p. 23); K-means clusters 89.2% faster at K = 50 with <0.25% gap (p. 24); alpha 0 vs 0.5: +11.3% true palatability for +2.5% cost (p. 26); epsilon < 0.25 keeps true palatability near 0.5 (pp. 27-28); RF/GBM with P = 25: 44.87 / 133.13 min average, 4 h limit leaves 1.02% / 5.21% gaps, 4 GBM runs infeasible (pp. 55-56); column selection flat to 5 x 10^5 points with MOSEK (pp. 51-52). Chemotherapy: temporal split, ground-truth ensemble scoring, feasible cohorts only (85 of 96 by my inference from Table 6): any-DLT satisfaction 0.847 -> 0.941, predicted survival +11.40%, DLT-only constraint worsens blood and infection (Table 6, p. 33); toxicity R^2 at most 0.268 (p. 58). App. E: beats JANOS on its own problem with logistic regression (pp. 60-61); solves EML's ANN1 with a 10-node ReLU net in 19.4 s (pp. 61-62).
positioning: Follows Fajemisin et al. 2021 (three of its authors) and Biggs et al.'s hull idea (pp. 6, 13-14, 38); JANOS/EML called restricted then tested on their own problems (p. 4; App. E); Verwer et al. similar, merits on each side (p. 12); prescriptive analytics incl. Bertsimas-Kallus uses predictions as inputs, this paper embeds models (p. 5); predict-then-optimize weakness conceded (p. 35); Optimal Trees described as approximating globally optimal trees (p. 10). For the skill's Roundtable Card (Leyffer, surrogates outside their data): the trust region already confines solutions to the data hull and measures how far outside it the learned constraint holds (pp. 13-15, 27-28).
writing: Abstract opens with a foundation claim (p. 1); two concrete examples before any symbol (p. 2); coins 'constraint learning' (p. 3); numbered contributions with a GitHub link (pp. 5-6); hypothesis stated before robustness experiments (p. 25); specific hedges (no best parameter setting, p. 26; clinical guidance for infeasible cohorts, p. 32); adoption vision for modelling software (p. 35); 'high-quality prescriptions' (p. 1) rests on simulator and ensemble scoring (pp. 19, 32); sign slip min y_OS (pp. 29-30).
limits_future: Limits: point predictions and misspecification only mitigated (p. 35); no unobserved confounding assumed (pp. 29, 35); counterfactual evaluation hard (p. 32); trust region costs time (pp. 23-24); column selection not inside branch and bound (p. 24); embedded ensembles blow up run time (pp. 55-56). Future: causal inference; robust optimization for prediction uncertainty of general ML models (pp. 34-35), taken up by S266 (S266 pp. 16-17).

method_links.note: Learns inside the decision instead of plugging in predictions (p. 5); the hull of past regimens shapes the class and doubles as 'clinically reasonable' treatment (p. 30); prescriptions judged against the regimens actually given (pp. 32-33); evaluation limits stated (pp. 29, 32, 35). Variant parts: model-based decision metric (ground-truth ensemble, simulator), no field test, and WFP's experts' rules replaced rather than duelled (p. 19). Aside for SKILL Heuristic 5, which cites this DOI: v3 learns constraints from decision-outcome data, not an optimizer's strategy for repeated online solves (pp. 1-9); Heuristic 6's data asset (the 2016 trial database) is reused (pp. 27-28, 56).

Class-keeping devices chosen on purpose: MIO-representable learners with linear constraints and linear SVMs only (pp. 9, 42), hull by weights not facets (p. 14), epsilon-CH norm limited to 1, 2 or inf to preserve the class (p. 18), parallel LOs for a lone tree (pp. 11-12); Wolfe-dual pricing (pp. 48-51); boundary printed by ensemble run times and gaps (pp. 55-56). The trained model is embedded exactly; the approximation is in the learning. Big-M tightened per split (p. 44) but stronger ReLU formulations only mentioned (p. 45; Tension T4).

Conservativeness of learned constraints gets explicit knobs (alpha, epsilon, P, K) handed to the end user (pp. 6, 26, 34) with printed price curves (Figure 7 p. 27, Figure 8 p. 28, Table EC.5 p. 55); but no solution-independent bound: the price is measured against a simulator's ground truth instead of proven.

Exact MIO solves with solver version and machine (pp. 22-23), time limit with remaining MIP gaps reported (p. 55), duel against JANOS and EML on their own test problems (pp. 59-62); no warm start or incumbent heuristic, and the JANOS duel uses logistic regression only (p. 61).

Programme continuity: reuses the 2016 chemotherapy data asset (S078) and Optimal Trees (pp. 10, 27-28, 56), sits beside Wiberg's constraint-learning thesis (S536, metadata), ships OptiCL as an adoption channel (p. 5), and is extended by S266.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: data convex hull as trust region
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Prescriptions confined to the hull of observed decisions and contexts, written with weights, clustered for low-density regions, enlarged by a norm ball; also encodes clinically reasonable treatments and dose logic
Ensemble violation limit over P bootstrapped or multi-class learners; S266 adds robust counterparts of learned parameters (S266 pp. 16-17); SKILL Method 5 cites a bootstrap-robust layer (S139)

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: score learned constraints where the optimizer lands
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: With a simulator as ground truth, validation MSE vs MSE at 100 optimal solutions without and with the trust region (e.g. CART 0.014 vs 0.273 vs 0.059)

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: held-out ground-truth ensemble for counterfactual scoring of prescriptions
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Temporal split; given and prescribed regimens both scored by an ensemble trained on all data; results only for cohorts with a feasible prescription

transferable: (D4) Embed a trained tree with one binary per leaf and big-M split constraints, computing each M by maximizing the split expression over the known constraints and trust region (eqs. (8)-(9), pp. 43-44); if the tree is the only learned constraint, solve one LP/MIO per feasible leaf in parallel (pp. 11-12, 44-45).

(D4) Keep solutions near the data with a convex hull written by convex-combination weights (eq. (2), p. 14), a union of cluster hulls with one binary per cluster (eq. (3), p. 14), and a 1-, 2- or inf-norm enlargement that stays in class (eq. (5), p. 18).
(D4) For a huge point set, start from about 100 points, price the rest by the KKT/Wolfe reduced cost and add the most negative one, always a hull vertex (Lemma 1, pp. 49-52).

(D4) Make a learned constraint robust to the learner by allowing at most an alpha share of P bootstrapped or different-class estimators to violate it; alpha = 0 and the mean constraint need no big-M (eq. (4), pp. 17, 47).
(D4) Embed classifiers by thresholding the logit at ln(tau/(1-tau)) instead of modelling the sigmoid, and an argmax big-M instead of a softmax (p. 46).
(D5) Report three errors per learner: validation, at the optimal solutions without a trust region, and with one, plus solve time with and without (Table 5, p. 23).
(D5) For MIOs with embedded ensembles, report mean, median and maximum time and, under a time limit, the shares optimal and feasible and the remaining gap (Table EC.7, p. 56).
coauthors: Donato Maragno and Holly Wiberg (equal contribution), S. Ilker Birbil, Dick den Hertog, Adejuyigbe O. Fajemisin (p. 1)

quotes.text: Our approach is distinct from existing work in that we directly embed ML models rather than extracting predictions, allowing us to optimize our decisions over the model.
and p set equal to 1,2 or ∞ to preserve the complexity of the optimization problem.

title: Global optimization: a machine learning approach
contribution: Extends OCTHaGOn: approximates the nonlinear or black-box constraints and objective of a global optimization problem by MIO-representable learners chosen per function (OCT-H, linear SVM, GBM, ReLU MLP), adds disagreement-driven adaptive sampling, robust counterparts of learned parameters and penalized relaxations, and repairs the MIO solution by projected gradient descent; better than OCTHaGOn in 39 of 77 MINLPLib instances and better or faster than BARON in 11 of 81 instances.
problem_entry: IO+HS+DA (ML engine, RO device): global solvers relax only specific primitives (BARON: exp, ln, x^a, b^x) and are generally ineffective on black-box or simulation-based constraints (p. 3); gradient, outer-approximation and branching methods each have named weaknesses (pp. 2-3); the group's own OCTHaGOn sometimes returns infeasible or suboptimal solutions (p. 3); general MINLP (1) with bounded variables in nonlinear constraints (pp. 2, 5).
key_idea: Replace each nonlinear constraint by a feasibility classifier and the objective by a regressor drawn from MIO-representable learners and picked by test accuracy or R^2 (pp. 7, 12), solve the MIO, then repair with momentum PGD (pp. 6, 8); new over OCTHaGOn: more learner classes, OCT-based adaptive sampling, robust counterparts of trained parameters, penalized relaxation (pp. 4, 7-8).
assumptions: Bounds on the variables of nonlinear constraints, otherwise inferred from linear constraints (pp. 5, 32); cheap constraint evaluations and automatic differentiation (pp. 32-33); explicit test problems only (p. 32); linear SVMs without kernels to keep the MIO linear (p. 9); multiplicative p-norm uncertainty of radius rho on learned coefficients (p. 16); small GBM ensembles (p. 17); bounded continuous nonconvex benchmarks (p. 23), plus one integer variable in the speed reducer (p. 31).
proof_devices: MIO embeddings of learned constraints: linear SVM as one linear constraint (eq. (5), p. 9); trees as leaf polyhedra with a big-M disjunction and epsilon for strict inequalities, feasibility y_DT >= 0.5 (eqs. (6)-(8), p. 10); GBM as a weighted tree sum (eq. (10), p. 11); ReLU MLP big-M with a positive-logit test (eq. (12), p. 12)

OCT sampling: K OCT-H trees on random subsets, disagreement set |P(x) - N(x)| <= K tau, intersected leaf polyhedra on which disagreement is guaranteed, hit-and-run sampling inside (eqs. (16)-(19), pp. 13-15)
Penalized-slack relaxation used only when the MIO is infeasible (eq. (20), pp. 15-16); feasibility whenever the original problem is feasible asserted without argument (p. 15)

Robust counterparts of trained parameters under multiplicative p-norm uncertainty with the dual norm (eqs. (21)-(24), pp. 16-17, via Bertsimas-den Hertog [24]); zero coefficients stay zero so parallel splits stay parallel (p. 16); L1/L-inf stay linear, L2 conic quadratic (p. 22)
Projected gradient descent repair with conditional momentum and second-order information (pp. 8, 22)
No convergence, approximation or complexity result; no global-optimality guarantee, admitted (p. 32)
experiments: 2-D example: MLP 0.97 and OCT 0.99 accuracy, MIO -1.108 then PGD to the global optimum -1.1497 (pp. 19, 22). 77 MINLPLib instances (1-110 variables), 1500 s, laptop, Julia 1.6.2, Gurobi 8.1, BARON 2021.01.13, best of a (rho, lambda) grid (p. 24): Base beats OCTHaGOn's gap in 39 and loses in 4; BARON optimal in 73; GoML better or faster than BARON in 9 (p. 25). My Table 1 tallies: Base infeasible in 9 rows (three of four 110-variable instances), NonCVX fully offloaded to Gurobi in 39, BARON median 0.2 s vs Base 37.4 s, 4 of 5 time wins against BARON runs at the 1500 s limit (pp. 26-27). Attribution: improved in 11/14/13 instances, 74-vs-77 inconsistency, robustness often infeasible (p. 28). Quadratic-sigmoid n = 50, 70: GoML gap <= 6.56% and <= 0.8% vs BARON >= 99.9% and >= 99.8%, one instance per size (p. 30). Speed reducer: IPOPT 4.2 s vs GoML 37 s at the same objective (p. 31).
positioning: Even-handed review of CONOPT, outer approximation (Duran-Grossmann; Bergamini, Grossmann et al.), BARON (Ryoo-Sahinidis) and ANTIGONE (Misener-Floudas), all very effective on some problem types (pp. 2-3); framed as an extension of the group's OCTHaGOn, whose shortfall motivates it (pp. 3-5); Constraint Learning (S097) 'a very relevant' work and OCTHaGOn its adaptation (p. 4); self-cited core [7], [8], [9], [16], [24] (pp. 34-35). A documented contact point with MINLP-team guests Sahinidis, Misener and Grossmann, with BARON as the opponent (pp. 24-27).
writing: Contributions (i)-(iv) (p. 4); eight-step pipeline labelled same / enhanced / new against the predecessor (pp. 7-8); a two-variable example walks every step (pp. 17-23); counts out of 77 (p. 25); hedges at both ends ('despite its approximate nature', pp. 5, 32) and a concrete Limitations subsection (pp. 32-33); but the title and 'new in the global optimization literature' (p. 33) sit beside BARON's 73 of 77 and no global guarantee (pp. 25, 32): Tension T6.
limits_future: Limits (pp. 32-33): no global-optimality guarantee, solutions may be suboptimal or infeasible; untested on true black-box constraints; bounds required; cheap evaluations and AD assumed (finite differences offered); OCT-H training the bottleneck, restricted to small problems; training time linear in nonlinear constraints; MIO time grows with deeper learners; no GoML code link in v1 (p. 24). Future work only broad: 'still a work in progress', applications without explicit formulations (pp. 32-33).

method_links.note: Class kept on purpose (linear SVMs keep the MIO linear, p. 9; L1/L-inf robust sets stay linear and L2 becomes conic quadratic, p. 22; constraints Gurobi takes exactly are passed through, p. 23), but the known problem is approximated by learned surrogates rather than written exactly (pp. 7, 12-13); boundary printed (p. 33).

Duels BARON on its home benchmark with version, limit and machine and prints BARON's 73 of 77 (pp. 24-25), plus OCTHaGOn and IPOPT (pp. 25, 31); MIO then PGD repair (p. 8); no certificate, admitted (p. 32), yet 'GOpt' labels (p. 24; Tension T1); best of a grid against one BARON run with time accounting unstated, and 4 of 5 time wins against BARON runs at the 1500 s limit (my Table 1 count, pp. 24-28).

rho prices robustness to learning error and lambda prices relaxation (pp. 8, 16, 22), but rho is tuned per instance to the best objective with no price curve (p. 24); the bad case appears only as counts and one sentence: robustness often makes the MIO infeasible (p. 28).

Programme lineage in one reference list: OCT (2017) -> OCTHaGOn (S298) -> Constraint Learning (S097) -> GoML, with the 2022 RO book's tools and an ORC co-author; also SKILL Heuristic 4 evidence (Inf rows, BARON's sub-second times, harmful enhancements and IPOPT's faster time printed in the body, pp. 26-28, 31).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Committee of OCT-H trees on subsamples, disagreement threshold, intersected leaf polyhedra, hit-and-run inside; improved the gap in 14 instances

Robust optimization on trained parameters rather than data, with multiplicative sets that keep sparsity; improved 11 instances but often made the MIO infeasible; follows S097's stated open problem (S097 p. 35)
Robustness and relaxation act on the embedding, so the (rho, lambda) grid re-solves without retraining; sampling and training take over 95% of the time in many cases

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: learn only what the solver cannot take exactly
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Linear constraints pass straight to the MIO; GoML NonCVX also passes convex and nonconvex quadratic constraints to Gurobi (39 of 77 rows fully offloaded by my count); compare S097's explicit f, g beside learned h (S097 p. 7)

transferable: (D2) For each awkward constraint, learn a feasibility classifier from a menu of MIO-representable learners chosen by held-out accuracy, and pass every constraint the solver handles exactly straight through (pp. 7, 12, 23).
(D4) Adaptive sampling: train K trees on random subsets, select points with |P(x) - N(x)| <= K tau, intersect their leaf polyhedra and hit-and-run sample inside (pp. 13-15).

(D4) Robustify a learned linear rule with multiplicative uncertainty, beta-bar^T x - rho ||beta-bar (elementwise) x||_q, which keeps zero coefficients zero and stays linear for L1 or L-inf (pp. 16, 22).
(D4) Infeasibility fallback: solve first without slacks; if infeasible, re-solve with penalized slacks u >= 0 (pp. 15-16).
(D5) Put robustness and relaxation knobs after training so a hyperparameter grid only re-embeds and re-solves (p. 24).
(D5) Bound unknown optima with the rival solver's lower bound and the best feasible point of either method (p. 30).
(D5) Attribution table: switch each enhancement on and off and count instances improved and unchanged, and add the worse row that Table 2 lacks (p. 28).
coauthors: Georgios Margaritis (MIT Operations Research Center, p. 1)

quotes.text: In our approach, however, we will use RO to deal with uncertainty not in the model data, but in the trained model parameters.
Since the method relies on ML-based approximations of the original problem, it does not necessarily produce globally optimal solutions.
